papers.title: Capturing additional variance in impact of adolescent depression from free text: proof of concept and preliminary results
papers.abstract: Depression in adolescents has grown in prevalence in the past decade. Despite indications of differences in symptom presentation, measurement properties, and treatment response between adolescents and adults, research is dominated by adult participants. Qualitative work has identified symptomatic and functional domains important to depressed adolescents and those around them; however, there remains little quantitative evidence of how these domains relate to the functional impact of the disorder. In this preregistered study, we use adolescent self-report (n = 153) and parent-report (n = 106) responses in the depression section of the Development and Well-Being Assessment (DAWBA) to examine what information relevant to reported depression impact may be missing from its structured symptom-scale. We apply Large Language Models (LLMs) to participant free-text answers to extract information on a taxonomy of 80 outcomes. Through a sequential residual stacking framework that estimates incremental information in symptom sum-scores (S ), item-level symptom-scale answers (Q), and LLM-derived text representations (T ), we find that parent text contains information relevant to their report of depression impact that is not available in the structured symptom-scale, with the largest contributions concentrated in functioning-related domains (e.g., professional responsibilities, social exclusion, autonomy, coping). No such evidence was found in adolescent self-reports. Given the moderate sample size, these results are preliminary. Nonetheless, we provide a proof-of-concept framework for extracting information from open-ended free text in large existing datasets, and estimating incremental information across sources, which could be applied to uncover specific aspects of adolescent mental disorders across populations.

papers.title: Polydrug use and recreational motives are associated with lower posttraumatic symptoms in survivors of a mass trauma event
papers.abstract: Objective: Drug use after trauma is common, but polydrug use patterns, motives, and associations with subsequent symptoms are poorly understood. We examined these associations among mass-casualty terror attack survivors, 72% of whom used drugs immediately before trauma exposure. Methods: Survivors of the October 7, 2023 Nova Festival attack reported use of six drug types (alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, psychedelics) and motives (avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication, sleep, recreation) longitudinally at three timepoints (TP): 1-6 months (N=772), 8-12 months (N=453), and 17-24 months (N=302) post-attack. Separate latent class analyses of TP2 data characterized drug use, motives, and their combination. Linear regression and mixed-effects models examined associations between class membership and PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, adjusting for age, sex, time since trauma, and TP1 PCL-5 scores. Results: At TP2, 70% reported polydrug use, 17% used one drug, and 13% reported no use. The high drug-load class (mean 4.6 drug types) had lower PCL-5 scores than the low drug-load class (mean 1.5 drug types); this difference was evident among participants using [≥]4 drug types and persisted through TP3. The self-medication-motive class had higher PCL-5 scores than the recreational-motive class. In joint analyses, recreational-motive users at both low and high drug loads had lower PCL-5 scores than participants reporting self-medication motives and primarily cannabis use. Conclusions: Polydrug use was common among the mass-trauma survivors in our study. Self-medication motives were associated with higher PTSD symptom severity than recreational motives. Unexpectedly, higher polydrug use was associated with lower PTSD symptom scores.

papers.title: Integrated Metabolomics Identifies Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Oxidative Membrane Remodeling, and Reduced Lipophilic Antioxidant Defenses in First-Episode Simple Dysmood Disorder
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolomic abnormalities in major depression have largely been investigated at the level of individual metabolites. We hypothesized that coordinated metabolic pathways, rather than isolated biomarkers, characterize first-episode simple dysmood disorder (FE-SDMD). Methods: Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics was performed in plasma from 44 FE-SDMD patients and 44 healthy controls. Differential metabolites were identified using Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction and integrated with complementary machine-learning approaches. Curated metabolites were grouped into biologically informed functional modules, validated using principal component analysis, and examined in relation to clinical phenome dimensions, adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), and negative life events (NLEs). Results: Of 450 detected metabolites, 298 remained significant after FDR correction and 240 additionally met fold-change criteria. Complementary feature-selection methods yielded a consensus panel of 20 biologically relevant metabolites that discriminated FE-SDMD from controls across multivariate and machine-learning analyses. Six functional modules revealed increased oxidative membrane remodeling, gut-liver dysfunction, mitochondrial bioenergetic dysfunction, reduced lipophilic antioxidant defenses and glucocorticoid metabolism, and altered dietary phytochemical metabolism. ACEs, particularly emotional neglect, and NLEs were associated with greater abnormalities across all modules. Gut-liver and mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, NLEs, and/or ACEs explained substantial variance in overall depression severity (66%), physiosomatic symptoms (41%), and suicidal ideation (43%). Conclusions: Functional metabolic modules provide a biologically interpretable systems-biology framework linking metabolomic abnormalities, psychosocial adversity, and clinical phenotypes, supporting the neuroimmune-metabolic-oxidative (NIMETOX) model of depression.

papers.title: Decision-Making Under Stress, Biological Stress Responses, and Risk for Suicidal Behavior in Young Adults
papers.abstract: Background: Stress may influence decision-making processes relevant to suicidal behavior, yet few studies have examined risky decision-making and expected value (EV) sensitivity under stress longitudinally among young adults at elevated suicide risk. Methods: Participants included 233 young adults (18-30 years) with recent suicide attempts (n=55), suicidal ideation (n=59), psychiatric controls (n=71), and healthy controls (n=48). Hair cortisol concentration, circulating inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1ra, TNF-alpha), Stressful Cups Task, and clinical measures were assessed at baseline, 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups. Results: Participants with a history of suicide attempts showed greater reductions in risky choices under stress over time compared to healthy controls. Greater reductions in EV sensitivity under stress relative to neutral conditions predicted subsequent suicidal behavior. Higher C-reactive protein (CRP) was associated with fewer risky choices under both neutral and stress conditions, while higher interleukin-6 (IL-6) was associated with fewer risky choices under neutral conditions. Higher interleukin-10 (IL-10) was associated with greater reductions in risky choices under stress relative to neutral conditions over time. No significant associations were observed for hair cortisol concentrations (HCC). Conclusions: Stress-related changes in risky decision-making and reduced EV sensitivity may contribute to vulnerability to suicidal behavior. These findings highlight the importance of assessing decision-making under stress and examining inflammatory processes as potential mechanisms underlying suicide risk.

papers.title: Delayed-centrifugation blood collection tube for remote blood biomarker assessment
papers.abstract: Introduction: Plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and amyloid-{beta} 42 (A{beta}42) are advancing toward clinical use for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their reliability can be impacted by preanalytical handling. Although alternative collection tubes with distinct stabilization strategies --P100 (protease inhibitor) and HEMAcollect (hemolysis/platelet-activation minimization) --have been developed to stabilize plasma proteins, how well they preserve these markers remains unresolved; we therefore compared both against fresh standard EDTA tubes. Methods: In 40 participants, plasma p-tau217 and A{beta}42 were measured (Lumipulse) in paired fresh EDTA, P100, and HEMAcollect samples after 5-day ambient storage. We assessed concentration change, rank-order preservation (Spearman {rho}), percentage difference, and diagnostic classification under the p-tau217/A{beta}42 ratio and p-tau217 alone. Results: P100 preserved p-tau217 favorably, with high rank-order correlation ({rho}=0.98) and a modest median change (+12.1%), and its classification agreement with fresh EDTA reached 97.5% using p-tau217 alone. HEMAcollect showed greater p-tau217 signal loss (-57.5%). A{beta}42 was reduced in both tubes (-72.8% P100; -95.5% HEMAcollect) with loss of rank order, so neither preserved the p-tau217/A{beta}42 ratio. Discussion: Stability was tube- and analyte-specific, and P100 consistently outperformed HEMAcollect --preserving p-tau217 rank order while HEMAcollect reduced signal across analytes. Although neither tube preserved the A{beta}42-dependent ratio, P100 shows potential for p-tau217-based workflows. Preanalytical stability must be established analyte by analyte before alternative tubes enter clinical AD diagnosis.

papers.title: Dyslexia extends beyond reading difficulties: genetic links with social functioning and well-being
papers.abstract: Dyslexia is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in reading and spelling. Although social and emotional challenges have been reported in individuals with dyslexia, the genetic relationships between dyslexia, social functioning, and well-being remain poorly understood. We combined phenotypic and genetic data from the Lifelines cohort with publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics. Associations between dyslexia and social traits were examined using a multi-layered approach encompassing complementary methods, including phenotypic correlation analyses, polygenic score (PGS) analyses, linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC), and bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Correlation analyses revealed significant phenotypic and genetic correlations between dyslexia and several social traits, including lower levels of life satisfaction, higher levels of loneliness, and less collegial support on the work floor. PGS analyses demonstrated that genetic liability to dyslexia predicted lower life satisfaction and reduced support from colleagues in the workplace, whereas none of the social-based PGSs predicted dyslexia. Bidirectional MR analyses provided evidence that genetic liability to dyslexia contributes to increased loneliness and social isolation, while no evidence was found for causal effects of social-interaction or well-being traits on dyslexia. Together, our results consistently supported a directional relationship from dyslexia toward social and well-being outcomes. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that dyslexia shares genetic influences with social interaction and well-being traits and suggest that genetic liability for dyslexia contributes to adverse (psycho)social outcomes. These results extend the impact of dyslexia beyond literacy-related difficulties and highlight the importance of providing social and structural support to individuals with dyslexia throughout the lifespan.

papers.title: State-independent functional connectomic architecture captures transdiagnostic network alterations and clinical variation
papers.abstract: Background: Psychiatric disorders show substantial overlap across diagnostic categories while differing markedly in clinical expression. Whether these shared abnormalities and individual differences are embedded in stable functional brain architecture rather than in state-specific connectivity remains unclear. Methods: We integrated functional connectomes across one resting-state and six task-based fMRI conditions in 377 participants from the YaleNeuroConnect cohort, including 223 healthy controls and 154 individuals with psychiatric disorders. Principal component analysis was applied to each participant's functional connectivity data across the seven states to derive a state-independent connectivity representation. Network-based statistics then identified components showing significant case-control differences. Cross-state consistency was assessed, and findings were validated in an independent UCLA cohort of 177 participants. Associations between component expression and clinical measures were further examined within the Yale psychiatric group. Results: Cross-paradigm connectivity revealed two reproducible patterns of state-independent network alteration. One pattern showed reduced connectivity among limbic, somatomotor and salience systems, whereas the other showed stronger cerebellar coupling with limbic and somatomotor systems. Both patterns showed consistent case-control differences across functional states and generalized to an independent UCLA cohort. Their clinical relevance, however, differed. Greater expression of the cerebello-cortical connectivity pattern was associated with lower positive affect, greater psychopathology and more everyday executive difficulties, whereas the reduced limbic-somatomotor-salience connectivity pattern showed no significant clinical associations. Conclusions: These findings delineate a stable reorganization of large-scale functional architecture across psychiatric disorders and suggest that broadly expressed psychiatric abnormalities and individual clinical variation may be differentially represented within the altered connectome.

papers.title: Frontoparietal functional connectivity underlies top-down attention in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: Patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment frequently show attention problems such as reduced top-down control, the ability to ignore task-irrelevant information. It is unclear whether this reduction corresponds with decreased brain connectivity. We aimed to determine whether and how differences in functional connectivity, or the correlated activity between brain areas, explain differences in top-down control in amnestic mild cognitive impairment. We conducted a case-control study with 26 patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (58-91 years; 10 women) and 29 age-matched healthy older adults (60-79 years; 9 women). All patients and control participants underwent neuropsychological assessment to confirm diagnosis and healthy cognitive status, respectively. We used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 3T to analyse functional connectivity. Top-down control was estimated with a 'theory of visual attention'-based verbal partial-report task (parameter ; higher indicates poorer control). We identified visual and attention-relevant functional brain networks and tested for differences between patients and controls while controlling for age and gender. Compared with healthy control participants, patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment showed lower functional connectivity in the left frontoparietal attention network and in one visual network and worse top-down control (t(37.43) = -2.24, p = 0.031). The reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network, but not the visual network, significantly correlated with top-down control across all participants ({rho} = -0.33, p = 0.003) and in the patient group ({rho} = -0.48, p = 0.014). Moreover, connectivity in the frontoparietal network mediated the relationship between amnestic mild cognitive impairment and top-down control . These results link lower frontoparietal connectivity to worse attentional control in patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Worse control reflects inefficient attentional selection and increasing distraction by irrelevant information during perceptual processing and encoding into working memory. Overall, this implicates a role for the frontoparietal network in maintaining cognitive control or, more generally, supporting cognitive functioning in older adults with emerging cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Evidence For Clinical Utility of a Dimensional Measure of Autistic Traits in Toddlers
papers.abstract: Objective: The Video-Referenced Rating of Reciprocal Social Behavior (vrRSB), a parent-report metric of quantitative autistic traits (QATs) in toddlers, leverages an innovative video scoring achor to reliably measure heritable, continuous varriation in autistic traits within the general population. However, the vrRSB's ability to distinguish toddlers with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has not been formally tested. Here we compared vrRSB scores in children with and without ASD in two samples: a community-ascertained research sample (RS) recruiting toddlers with and without ASD and a clinically referred sample (CS) consisting of toddlers with concerns for ASD. Methods: T-tests and logistic regressions indexed differences in vrRSB scores for toddlers with versus without ASD in both samples (RS: nASD=92, nnon-ASD=456; CS: nASD=127, nnon-ASD=44). Regression models additionally tested for differential functioning of the vrRSB relative to sex and race. ROC analysis compared classification performance of the vrRSB versus the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT). Results: Autistic toddlers exhibited significantly higher vrRSB scores in both samples: Cohen's dRS=3.68; Cohen's dCS=1.04, ps .293). The vrRSB exhibited similar area under the curve as the M-CHAT in both samples with higher sensitivity in the CS. Conclusion: Toddler QATs show predictive validity for autism diagnostic outcome. Consistent performance across sex and racial groups suggests promise for generalizable clinical interpretation and implementation. High sensitivity of the vrRSB supports utility for secondary screening in specialty evaluations.

papers.title: Prevalence and Sociodemographic Correlates of Depression and Thoughts of Self-Harm Among Adolescents in Five Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Evidence from the Demographic and Health Survey Program
papers.abstract: Background Adolescence is a critical period for the onset of depression and self-harm, yet comparable, nationally representative estimates from low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remain scarce. Existing evidence relies heavily on school-based samples, excluding out-of-school adolescents. The recently available data from Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Mental Health Module offers an opportunity to address this gap. Methods and findings We analysed data from 16,269 adolescents aged 15-19 years across five DHS surveys: Bangladesh (2022), Lesotho (2023-24), Mozambique (2022-23), Nepal (2022), and Zambia (2024). Probable depression was defined as a PHQ-9 score [≥]10, and thoughts of death or self-harm as any endorsement of PHQ-9 item 9. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence by country, sex, and age, examined symptom profiles, and used sex- and country-specific modified Poisson regression to identify sociodemographic correlates. The country-normalised pooled prevalence was 3.9% (95% CI 3.4-4.5) for probable depression, ranging from 0.6% in Zambia to 6.5% in Mozambique, and 7.0% (95% CI 6.4-7.7) for thoughts of death or self-harm, ranging from 3.1% to 10.2%, respectively. Girls had higher prevalence than boys for both depression (4.9% vs 1.9%) and thoughts of death or self-harm (8.6% vs 3.9%), although sex differences varied across countries. No consistent age gradient emerged. Associations with household composition, marital and parental status, urban residence, education, and wealth were heterogeneous across settings. Interpretation is limited by the lack of population-specific PHQ-9 validation and cross-country measurement invariance testing, the inability of item 9 to distinguish passive death wishes from suicidal ideation, the restriction to ever-married girls in Bangladesh, and the cross-sectional design. Conclusions Across five LMICs, PHQ-9-defined probable depression was relatively uncommon, while thoughts of death or self-harm affected approximately one in fourteen adolescents, particularly in girls. Substantial cross-country variation highlights the need for context-sensitive adolescent mental health surveillance and prevention, including out-of-school populations, supported by repeated household surveys and locally validated measures.

papers.title: Understanding How the Self-Regulation in Sport Practice Survey is Received by Mental Performance Consultants for Prospective Use in Applied Practice
papers.abstract: This study explored Mental Performance Consultants (MPCs) perspectives on the prospective use of the Self-Regulation in Sport Practice (SRSP) survey when consulting adolescent athletes. Twelve Canadian MPCs completed mock SRSP surveys and interviews about the surveys content and what they anticipated they could gain by using it with clients. Most of the MPCs claimed they could use the SRSP as an applied consulting resource. They believed that the SRSP could benefit the self-awareness of athletes and serve their information-gathering during case conceptualization. Most MPCs foresaw framing and enlarging SRSP statements/scores in joint discussion with a client, as part of triangulation, with some valuing the survey metrics for athletes and oneself. However, MPCs were philosophically divided on survey use, exposing uncertainty and negative preconceptions for some around quantitative assessment.

papers.title: Examining the Etiological Specificity of Genetic Risk for Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Consumption through Symptom-Level Mediation Analyses
papers.abstract: IntroductionPolygenic scores (PGSs) for alcohol use disorder (AUD) may capture genetic liability related to alcohol consumption as well as broader transdiagnostic traits, including impulsivity, aggression, and neuroticism. However, the extent to which these traits account for associations between an AUD PGS and the presentation of AUD symptoms remains unclear. Thus, to better understand the genetic influences captured by an AUD PGS, the present study used mediation analyses to examine whether these transdiagnostic traits differentially mediate the relations between PGSs for AUD and individual AUD symptoms while conducting a parallel analysis using a PGS of alcohol consumption to examine differences in the genetic influences underlying AUD and consumption. MethodParticipants were drawn from the UCSF Family Alcoholism Study. Separate mediation models examined maximum habitual drinks (N = 1,611) and MMPI-2 Personality Psychopathology Five (PSY-5) scales (N = 1,464) as mediators of the association between AUD/alcohol consumption PGSs and individual AUD symptoms. Covariates included sex, age, and 10 ancestry principal components. Observations were modeled as clustered within families, and a Bonferroni correction was applied (p < .0045). ResultsRelations between the AUD PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks and partially mediated by neuroticism for nearly all symptoms, but not by other PSY-5 scales. Relations between the alcohol consumption PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks alone, with no mediation observed through any personality psychopathology measure. DiscussionCurrent AUD and alcohol consumption PGSs appear to capture genetic liability that operates predominantly through alcohol consumption. However, the AUD PGS may capture genetic influences on broader transdiagnostic factors as well, with neuroticism acting as a partial mediator. Thus, etiological interpretations of the AUD PGS as solely a measure of AUD risk should be made cautiously.

papers.title: Exploratory Symptom Profiles and Clinical Correlates in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Retrospective Study Using the Wender-Reimherr Adult Attention Deficit Disorder Scale
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmotional dysregulation (ED) is a clinically relevant feature of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), but its relationship to clinical burden remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to describe latent symptom profiles and compare clinical and sociodemographic characteristics of adults assigned to classes with elevated probabilities in emotion-related domains with those assigned to the remaining classes. MethodsThis retrospective cross-sectional study included 749 adults with ADHD from a specialized outpatient clinic. Latent class analysis was performed on 28 items of the clinician-rated Wender-Reimherr Adult Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (WRAADDS). Classes with elevated probabilities in temper, affective lability, and emotional overreactivity were grouped post hoc as an exploratory ADHD+ED group; the remaining classes formed the ADHD group. These labels do not denote clinical diagnoses. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative groupings and adjustment for core ADHD symptom severity. ResultsA six-class solution was retained. Under the primary grouping, 60.9% of participants were assigned to ED-related classes (24.6%-77.0% across alternative groupings). The ADHD+ED group showed greater psychological distress, depressive symptoms, and functional impairment; these differences persisted after adjustment for core symptom severity. Differences on several subscales of the Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) also remained, whereas differences in broader ADHD self-report scores and the number of comorbid diagnoses did not. The small difference in drug-use screening scores was not robust in sensitivity analyses; alcohol-use screening scores and sociodemographic characteristics did not differ significantly. ConclusionsAssignment to the exploratory ED-related group was associated with greater psychological distress, depressive symptoms, and functional impairment. The proportion assigned depended on the grouping and should not be interpreted as an ED prevalence estimate. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference; the single-center sample and exclusion of severe psychiatric comorbidities limit generalizability; and the shared WRAADDS basis limits independent interpretation of WRAADDS-derived group differences. Future research should use independent, dimensional measures of ED and longitudinal designs, and should evaluate interventions targeting emotion regulation in adults with ADHD.

papers.title: Statistical analysis plan for the feasibility trial assessing external trigeminal nerve stimulation versus sham stimulation for ADHD in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years (the eTNS4ADHD trial)
papers.abstract: BackgroundExternal trigeminal nerve stimulation (eTNS) is a non-invasive intervention being investigated as a potential treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents. The eTNS4ADHD trial aims to assess the feasibility of conducting a larger randomised clinical trial comparing active eTNS with sham stimulation. This paper presents the prespecified statistical analysis plan for the trial. MethodsThe eTNS4ADHD trial is a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised pilot and feasibility trial involving children and adolescents aged 7-17 years with ADHD. Participants are allocated to four weeks of active eTNS or sham stimulation. Feasibility outcomes include recruitment, treatment compliance, acceptability, follow-up completion, and concomitant treatment use. Exploratory clinical outcomes include ADHD symptoms, school absence, emotional lability, functional impairment, quality of life, sleep quality, and adverse events. All analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Feasibility outcomes will primarily be assessed using proportions with 95% confidence intervals, while exploratory clinical outcomes will be analysed using regression models or non-parametric methods, as appropriate. Two independent statisticians blinded to treatment allocation will conduct the analyses, and blinded conclusions will be prepared before unblinding. DiscussionThis statistical analysis plan was finalised before unblinding to promote transparency and minimise the risk of selective analyses and reporting. Given the feasibility design and limited statistical power, exploratory clinical findings will be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The results will inform the feasibility, outcome selection, sample size estimation, and statistical methodology of a future definitive randomised clinical trial evaluating eTNS for ADHD in children and adolescents. Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06655610.

papers.title: Maintaining EHR-based Predictive Clinical Decision Support in Mental Health against Temporal Shifts
papers.abstract: Electronic health record (EHR)-based risk prediction offers opportunities for early intervention in mental health, but models may remain in use as patient populations, care practices, and documentation change. Such temporal shifts can reduce predictive performance, while updating models from recent data alone may be unstable when adverse outcomes are uncommon. We developed Adversarial Drift-Aware Predictive Transfer (ADAPT), a distributionally robust approach to improve the temporal durability of mental health risk prediction. ADAPT uses variation in models estimated from previous calendar periods to characterize plausible changes in predictor-outcome relationships. Data from the current period constrain which historical patterns remain relevant, allowing the method to seek robustness against subsequent shifts while preserving contemporary discrimination. We retrospectively evaluated ADAPT using EHRs from 889,445 patients with mental health diagnoses at Mass General Brigham and Duke University Health System, covering one-year risk prediction for 28 outcomes. In the worst 20% of year-pair comparisons, ADAPT improved AUC over all comparators by 0.016-0.036 at Mass General Brigham, 0.011-0.018 at Duke, and 0.008-0.037 after transport. For suicide-attempt prediction, contemporary AUC at Mass General Brigham was 0.82 compared with 0.80 for the best comparator. Eight-year relative AUC degradation was 7.7%, compared with 12.1% for pooled-data training. These results suggest that information from prior temporal shifts can improve robustness to future changes without sacrificing predictive performance for current patients.

papers.title: Exploring the Attitudes, Barriers, Concerns, Differences, and Ethics (ABCDEs) of Healthcare Decision Making of Vagus Nerve Stimulation
papers.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is an established neuromodulation therapy approved for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and epilepsy, with growing interest in its application to other conditions. Despite demonstrated clinical efficacy, VNS remains underused in psychiatric care. This mixed-methods study examined stakeholder perceptions of VNS, focusing on access, stigma, ethical concerns, and acceptability across epilepsy, depression, heart failure (HF), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). We conducted six focus groups and 20 semi-structured interviews with patients, clinicians, and one support person, and integrated qualitative themes with quantitative data on stigma and treatment barriers. Participants revealed stark disparities in VNS adoption: epilepsy patients reported fewer insurance barriers, while TRD participants faced delayed approvals, high out-of-pocket costs, and limited access to specialty care. Depression stakeholders reported higher stigma scores and expressed greater reluctance to consider surgical treatment, despite possessing comparable knowledge to epilepsy stakeholders. Ethical concerns--particularly regarding informed consent and impaired decision-making--surfaced frequently in the context of TRD. Most participants agreed that the appropriateness of VNS should align with disease severity and impact on quality of life. Many cautiously supported VNS for HF and RA, provided strong efficacy data supports its use. Hope emerged as a consistent theme, especially among TRD participants seeking alternatives after exhausting other treatments. These findings underscore the need to address insurance barriers, reduce stigma, and enhance provider education. As VNS expands into new indications, policymakers and clinicians must implement reforms that promote equitable access, decentralized care, and ethically sound consent practices to ensure inclusive neuromodulation therapy adoption.

papers.title: Core schema instability in youth at clinical high risk for psychosis: within-person variability as an index of self-belief precision
papers.abstract: AimCore schemas are considered stable traits in clinical high risk (CHR) research. However, unexamined fluctuation may conceal belief changes that precede psychosis emergence. We examined whether schemas possess considerable within-person variability in CHR, and whether that variability exceeds that of controls. MethodsIn NAPLS-2, 411 CHR and 194 control participants completed the Brief Core Schema Scales (BCSS) at least three times across 24 months. Random-intercept models identified intraclass correlations in CHR. Bayesian censored location-scale models, correcting for floor scores and mean level differences, compared within-person SD between groups. ResultsWithin-person variance accounted for 41.3%-50.6% of BCSS variance in CHR. Latent within-person SD was greater in CHR on all four subscales, most for negative-self (ratio 1.71, 95% CrI [1.50, 1.94]). This variability was largely independent of shared improvement and psychotropic medication effects. ConclusionsCore schemas fluctuate substantially in CHR compared to controls, particularly in negative self-beliefs. Single baseline scores may understate schema-outcome associations.

papers.title: SPEECH FEATURES IN A DEVELOPMENTAL PERSPECTIVE: A SCREENING TOOL FOR PSYCHOSIS, DEPRESSION AND ANXIETY
papers.abstract: Language production provides a window into cognitive development, social cognition, and mental health. To translate this potential into clinical practice, we developed a scalable speech-based platform integrating graph-theoretical, psycholinguistic, and emotional features from brief spontaneous narratives to support developmental monitoring, mental wellness screening, and clinical decision-making. Normative developmental trajectories were derived from 2149 participants spanning 0-23 years of formal education. Narratives elicited using positively valenced pictures were transformed into word graphs to derive two composite indices: Narrative Complexity (NC), reflecting structural language organization, and Emotional Narrative Complexity (ENC), integrating narrative structure and emotional content. Both indices were modeled using asymptotic functions calibrated by schooling and converted into percentile-based normative curves. NC (R{superscript 2} = 0.29, {tau} = 7.77) and ENC (R{superscript 2} = 0.31, {tau} = 6.97) increased with schooling, approaching saturation around middle school. These trajectories provide educationally calibrated references for evaluating linguistic and socioemotional development. Clinical utility was investigated in a transdiagnostic sample of 120 participants, comprising healthy controls (n = 38), mood disorders (n = 28), affective psychosis (n = 36), and non-affective psychosis (n = 18). Although ENC alone did not discriminate between symptom-risk or diagnostic groups, classifiers combining its constituent variables with education and sex achieved AUCs of 0.726 for symptom risk and 0.800 for diagnosis, increasing to 0.774 and 0.858, respectively, with additional linguistic features. Machine-learning models integrating graph-derived, psycholinguistic, and emotional features further estimated symptom dimensions assessed by PANSS, GAD-7, and PHQ-9, achieving AUCs of 0.74-0.92 across severity thresholds while maintaining sensitivity [≥] 0.80. Individual linguistic variables also differed significantly across symptom-severity strata, suggesting distinct associations with psychopathological dimensions. Together, these findings establish an integrated speech-based framework spanning normative developmental assessment, mental wellness screening, and symptom-informed clinical support. By combining educationally calibrated trajectories with interpretable linguistic features and machine learning, this approach offers scalable digital markers to identify atypical developmental patterns, inform preventive strategies, and assist clinical assessment and decision-making.

papers.title: Pupil size-resting state network coupling in major depressive disorder: a longitudinal iTBS study
papers.abstract: Altered central-peripheral autonomic nervous system communication plays a key role in major depressive disorder (MDD). In this context, pupillary dynamics may be considered a non-invasive peripheral proxy of treatment-related changes during intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) in MDD. However, the relationship between spontaneous pupillary fluctuations and the resting-state functional networks (RSNs) involved in MDD is still underexplored. Here, we investigated longitudinal changes in pupil-RSN coupling in patients with MDD undergoing an iTBS intervention. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging with concurrent pupillometry was acquired at four study visits. Group independent component analysis was used to estimate tonic pupil coupling with predefined RSNs of interest, along with a linear mixed-effects model to assess longitudinal changes in pupil size-RSN coupling and, exploratively, the effect of potential clinical and behavioral moderators. Among the examined RSNs, the left executive control network (lECN), including the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex as the cortical target of stimulation, exhibited a sustained reduction in positive pupil size coupling relative to baseline, irrespective of treatment order (active - sham). To determine whether this longitudinal change was accompanied by a more general change in pupil diameter, we additionally examined pupil size independently of RSNs. Pupil diameter decreased significantly from baseline, with greater decreases being positively associated with greater reductions in anxiety scores. Notably, reduction in anxiety symptoms were also positively correlated with reduction in depressive symptoms. Together, these findings suggest that longitudinal reductions in pupil-IECN coupling occur alongside reductions in pupil diameter that are associated with reductions in anxiety symptoms.

papers.title: Synaptic density (SV2A) tracks illness chronicity rather than symptom severity in major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Synaptic loss has been proposed as a key mechanism in major depressive disorder (MDD). Positron emission tomography with [{superscript 1}{superscript 1}C]UCB-J enables in vivo quantification of synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), a proxy marker of synaptic density. A landmark study by Holmes et al reported an inverse association between depression severity and SV2A binding in frontolimbic regions. As a replication, we examined this association in [{superscript 1}{superscript 1}C]UCB-J PET data from 34 unmedicated individuals with MDD, focusing on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and hippocampus. We found no support of an association between MADRS scores and SV2A binding in the primary regions of interest (r = 0.18-0.26, all p [≥] 0.15). Findings were similar in unadjusted and age- and sex-adjusted models. However, adjustment for duration of the current depressive episode and lifetime depressive episodes yielded positive associations across primary regions. In post hoc analyses, longer current episode duration, but not lifetime depressive episodes, was negatively associated with SV2A binding across primary regions. Thus, our findings did not support an association between depression severity and synaptic density, contrary to a previous report; instead, the exploratory findings suggest that SV2A binding may be related to episode duration rather than current symptom burden.

papers.title: Psilocybin, cognitive stability and drinking reduction in co-occurring alcohol use disorder and depression: a pilot secondary analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundChange in cognitive control is a candidate transdiagnostic mechanism of psychedelic therapy. One account predicts that, once acute effects resolve, psilocybin shifts control toward flexibility while sparing inhibition and working memory. A motivational account (PRISM) predicts that psilocybin increases the willingness to exert control rather than the ability to do so. We tested both in patients with co-occurring alcohol use disorder (AUD) and major depression. MethodsIn this secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of psilocybin for AUD with comorbid major depressive disorder (MDD; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04620759), a subset of participants (placebo n=13, psilocybin n=12) completed five cognitive tasks before drug administration and again about one week after it (mean 6.7 days, SD 1.1). Outcome measures spanned the stability-flexibility continuum. Free choice between levels of cognitive demand indexed the participants willingness to exert control. Effect sizes and Bayes factors were used to estimate drug effects and associations with change in drinking and depressive symptoms across 34 retest measures. ResultsRelative to placebo, psilocybin slowed responding in cued task switching (learning-phase RT d=1.01, BF10=7.7; switch trials d=1.12, BF10=17). Psilocybin effects on feedback-driven measures were inconsistent in direction (7 of 11 toward flexibility); the largest was on perseveration, which rose less with practice under psilocybin than under placebo (d=-0.79, BF10=1.1). Other drug effects on the 34 retest measures had inconclusive Bayes factors (BF10=0.40-2.4), and none survived false discovery rate correction. Demand avoidance, analyzed separately from the 34 measures, showed no detectable drug effect (BF01=2.0). Baseline demand avoidance showed no detectable relation to performance but tracked depressive symptoms (rs=.71, BF10=24). Drinking fell in both arms, and on 15 of 17 stability-flexibility measures change toward stability accompanied drinking reduction (stability composite rs=-.64, BF10=29; rs=-.43 when change was adjusted for baseline scores). Lower baseline working-memory span predicted larger drinking reductions (BF10=19-25). Depressive symptoms fell more after psilocybin than after placebo (PHQ-9, d=-0.88, BF10=2.7), but their change was not associated with cognitive change or predicted by working-memory span. ConclusionsAbout one week after dosing, psilocybin slowed cued task switching but had no consistent effect on feedback-driven flexibility, and there was no evidence of an effect on the willingness to exert effort. Drinking reduction was associated with increased, not reduced, cognitive stability, whereas improvement in depressive symptoms was not associated with cognitive change. These pilot estimates can guide adequately powered trials.

papers.title: Effect of food-cues on aMCC glutamate modulation during inhibitory control post weight loss intervention: a 1H fMRS study
papers.abstract: ObjectivePoor inhibitory control may decrease weight loss maintenance. The neurobiological mechanisms are poorly understood. We investigated whether glutamate modulation in the anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC) during response inhibition is impacted by food-cues and associated with self-reported behaviors and weight loss maintenance. Methods27 adults with overweight/obesity were recruited from a clinical weight management program. 1H fMRS (midline aMCC) was acquired during a visual-guided response inhibition task engaging two responding modes [non-selective (100% responses) or selective (withholding a response on 20% of trials)] applied with neutral (squares) or food/non-food cues. The impact of stimulus type on the aMCC glutamate modulation for each responding mode was assessed using a repeated measures GEE approach. Correlations were conducted between glutamate modulation, Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire scores, and long-term weight change. ResultsThe stimulus effect was significant during selective responding, driven by lower aMCC glutamate modulation during food/non-food cues. This glutamate modulation (selective; food/non-food) association with weight loss maintenance was a close trend (R2=0.15, p=0.054). The association with the TFEQ Cognitive Restraint was significant (R2=0.20, p=0.047). ConclusionsThese results demonstrate an impact of food/non-food cues during response inhibition on the neurobiology and associations with long-term weight loss maintenance and scores related to eating behaviors.

papers.title: Post-psychedelic and meditation-related challenges: a protocol for a mixed-methods longitudinal-observational study
papers.abstract: IntroductionPsychedelics and meditation are increasingly used for therapeutic and wellness purposes. However, research into adverse effects (AEs) has been limited, without adequate investigation of the nature, clinical characteristics, and diversity of persisting challenges following psychedelic use and meditation practice. This study aims to better characterize the clinical and contextual features of these challenges, describe their longitudinal course, and compare psychedelic-related challenges to meditation-related challenges, selected as comparator conditions given previously characterized phenomenological and contextual overlap between the two. Methods and AnalysisThis is a mixed-methods, enriched-sample, active-comparator (psychedelics vs. meditation) observational study comprising (1) a cross-sectional retrospective survey (N = 1,600), (2) a prospective 12-month longitudinal design involving six bimonthly surveys (n = 800), (3) 12 weeks of weekly ambulatory assessments combining quantitative symptom ratings with narrative voice report (n = 40), and (4) qualitative interviews (n = 60). Participants are recruited into two parallel arms of 800 each: individuals reporting psychedelic-related challenges and individuals reporting meditation-related challenges, defined as distress or impairment persisting after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or period of meditation practice have subsided. Data collection includes a tailored item pool aimed at capturing the symptoms and phenomenology of these challenges in detail, developed from qualitative research and collaboratively with stakeholders with lived experience. The World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0) and measures of agent/exposure, set, setting, and social response are administered to characterize biopsychosocial correlates and functional impacts of AEs. Initial analyses will describe the phenomenology, course, and functional impact of psychedelic- and meditation-related challenges, and evaluate the structure and psychometric properties of the novel item pool. The study will produce a publicly available de-identified dataset supporting subsequent analyses, such as correspondence with recognized clinical syndromes, trajectory characterization, and cross-arm comparison of measurement structure, reported in registered reports or preregistrations.

papers.title: "It was like a weird, paralysing thing": Understanding the development and consequences of emotionally based school non-attendance (EBSNA) through young people's and parents' experiences.
papers.abstract: Emotionally based school non-attendance (EBSNA) is an increasing concern, yet relatively little research has integrated young peoples and parents perspectives to understand how attendance difficulties develop and affect young people and their families. This qualitative study explored the development and consequences of EBSNA through the complementary experiences of young people and parents. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 parents and 16 young people aged 11-17 years who had experienced EBSNA. Young people could participate through either verbal or written interviews to support inclusive participation. Data were analysed using the Framework Method, with multiple researchers contributing to coding, charting and interpretation. Three overarching themes were identified: misalignment between young peoples needs and the school environment; becoming unable to attend school; and the wider impact of EBSNA. Across accounts, EBSNA developed gradually through interactions between individual needs and school environments, rather than being attributable to individual characteristics alone. Sensory, social, organisational and academic demands, particularly during the transition to secondary school, combined with unmet needs, bullying, punitive practices and difficulties establishing trusting relationships to progressively undermine psychological safety and belonging. As distress escalated, anxiety increasingly extended beyond specific school situations to school itself, eventually making attendance feel psychologically and physically impossible. Once established, absence created additional barriers to returning through lost confidence, disrupted friendships and concerns about falling behind. Despite substantial educational disruption, young people generally remained motivated to learn. EBSNA also had profound social and family consequences, including isolation, deteriorating parental wellbeing, disrupted family relationships and financial pressures. Findings conceptualise EBSNA as a dynamic socioecological process and highlight the importance of early, individualised responses that address unmet needs and create psychologically safe, inclusive and supportive school environments.

papers.title: Childhood adverse experiences associate with reduced brain CB1 endocannabinoid receptor availability in healthy controls and patients with first-episode psychosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe brain endocannabinoid system (ECS) is dysregulated in first-episode psychosis (FEP) but understanding of the nature and origins of ECS dysregulation in FEP is limited. The imprinting of developmental adversity and stress into the adult ECS has not been previously studied in humans. We tested the hypothesis that childhood adverse events (ACE) associate with decreased brain type-1 endocannabinoid receptor (CB1R) availability in patients with FEP and healthy controls (HC). MethodsCB1R availability was measured cross-sectionally in male and female patients with FEP (n=15), and healthy participants (n=20). Brain CB1R binding was measured with the selective CB1R radiotracer [18F]FMPEP-d2 using positron emission tomography (PET). Distribution volumes (VT) using metabolite corrected arterial input was a proxy of CB1R availability, which was measured in 13 functionally relevant regions of interest (ROI). ACE before the age of 16 were categorized as simple (0-1 events) or multiple ([≥] 2 events) using a Finnish population survey questionnaire. ResultsAn rmANOVA model of regional CB1R VT (ROI [~] sex + group + sex*group + ACE) indicated statistically significant associations of ACE (p<0.001), group (p=0.027) and sex*group interaction(p=0.018). The largest effect sizes of ACE on CB1R were seen in the amygdala (2=.37), temporal cortex (2=.35), hippocampus (2=.33) and insula (2=.31). DiscussionMultiple childhood adverse effects were associated with lower availability of temporo-limbic CB1R in adulthood in healthy participants and in patients with first-episode psychosis. These results corroborate previous results from pre-clinical studies, and expand the literature in showing that early adversity can be imprinted into the function of human brain in adulthood. The results have implications for studies on resilience and adaptation to stress as well as studies on vulnerability to psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of a Culturally Adapted Internet-Based Mental Health Promotion Intervention for Indonesian Undergraduate Students (LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh): A Protocol for a Single-Arm, Pre-Post Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMental health problems are highly prevalent among university students globally and in Indonesia, yet the vast majority do not receive adequate care. Whilst existing digital mental health interventions in Indonesia have primarily targeted students with clinically elevated symptoms, no prior study has evaluated an internet-based intervention designed to promote positive mental health among Indonesian university students. LifeHack is an internet-based guided self-help intervention developed to promote positive mental health as part of the Caring Universities initiative within the WHO World Mental Health-International College Student (WMH-ICS) framework. LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh is a culturally adapted Indonesian version, developed through a systematic adaptation process guided by Bernals Ecological Validity Model and the Heuristic Framework for Cultural Adaptation. Objectives: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted intervention, including its usability, participant satisfaction, adherence, and retention. Secondarily, it will examine preliminary signals of change in resilience, positive mental health, depression and anxiety symptoms, and coping strategies. MethodsThis protocol describes a single-arm pre-post feasibility study involving 50 undergraduate students aged 18 years or older from Universitas Padjadjaran and Universitas Jambi, Indonesia. Participants will receive the culturally adapted LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh, a self-paced web-based guided self-help intervention supported by asynchronous personalised feedback from trained e-coaches. Participants may select modules according to their individual needs and complete the intervention over a flexible period of 1-6 weeks. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T0), immediately following intervention completion or at the end of the six-week intervention period if participants have not previously indicated completion (T1), and three months after T1 (T2). Primary feasibility outcomes include usability, satisfaction, intervention adherence, retention, and intervention completion. Secondary outcomes include resilience, positive mental health, psychological distress, coping, and safety. Safety will be assessed through participant-reported negative effects and recorded adverse events identified through routine e-coach monitoring. Progression to a future randomised controlled trial will be evaluated using pre-specified traffic light criteria. Expected OutcomesFindings will inform the feasibility, cultural appropriateness, and preliminary effects of the adapted LifeHack intervention for Indonesian students. Results will guide potential progression to a fully powered randomised controlled trial. Trial RegistrationThai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR), TCTR20260530005--, registered on 9th May 2026 and updated on 17th August 2026

papers.title: Negotiating belonging and identity across the life course: A qualitative study using Social Identity Mapping with people with psychosis
papers.abstract: A core part of how we understand ourselves comes from the groups we feel we belong to. Having positive, meaningful group memberships, or "social identities", has been linked to better wellbeing in people diagnosed with psychotic disorders, yet little attention has been paid to how individuals with psychosis experience social identities and changes in belonging across the life course. Personal recovery in psychosis has been described as centred on identity and connection: it may be useful therefore to consider the experiences of people with psychosis from the perspective of the Social Identity Approach to Health (SIAH). This study used Social Identity Mapping (SIM) as the basis for semi-structured interviews (n = 28). Thematic analysis, conducted by a team drawing on wide-ranging expertise (lived experience, clinical psychiatry and social psychology), generated four themes: (1) Pre-symptom social identity conflict and non-belonging: "Im just something in-between"; (2) Psychosis tears identity apart: "The map would have been blank"; (3) Social identification is both a risk and a requirement for recovery: "Everyone wants to belong to some certain group or another"; and (4) Lack of identification with people with psychosis: "Do I feel a part of that group? Not really, no." This SIM-supported interview approach uncovered new insights into how people negotiate social identification before, during and after psychosis. Social identification may be a protective factor, and social identity-strengthening interventions should be evaluated as means of improving quality of life and social functioning.

papers.title: Familial factors inflate the estimated effects of genetic liability to ADHD on behavioural outcomes
papers.abstract: BackgroundPeople with ADHD have worse health, behavioural and social outcomes, widely interpreted as evidence that ADHD causes these harms, justifying early identification and treatment. But ADHD clusters in families, and conventional studies cannot separate the effect of a persons own ADHD from the family environment in which it arises. We used a family-based genetic design to distinguish the two. MethodsWe used up to 22 genome-wide significant variants associated with ADHD (38,691 cases, 186,843 controls) to estimate effects of genetic liability to ADHD on 16 health and behavioural outcomes. We compared population-based estimates with family-based estimates from within-sibship analyses of up to 164,220 siblings. We tested for heterogeneity between the designs, and applied sensitivity analyses. We involved individuals with lived experience of ADHD in interpreting the findings and shaping how the clinical/public-health implications were described. FindingsPopulation-based analyses implied that greater genetic liability to ADHD increased smoking, alcohol use and depressive symptoms, and reduced educational attainment, age at first child and cognitive performance. In family-based analyses, these effects attenuated. For example, the effect on number of depressive symptoms fell from 0{middle dot}059 SD (95% CI 0{middle dot}039, 0{middle dot}080) to 0{middle dot}002 SD (-0{middle dot}052, 0{middle dot}055), and age at first child increased from -0{middle dot}045 SD (-0{middle dot}058, -0{middle dot}033) to 0{middle dot}003 SD (-0{middle dot}040, 0{middle dot}047), with significant differences between designs (p=0{middle dot}048 and p=0{middle dot}034). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. InterpretationMuch of the excess health and behavioural burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD occurs, rather than an individuals own ADHD. Interventions targeting the individual might not reduce these outcomes as much as expected. Distinguishing such effects requires family-based designs. FundingMedical Research Council, UK Research and Innovation, Research Council of Norway, US National Institute of Mental Health, and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSAttention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and higher genetic liability to ADHD, are associated with a wide range of adverse health, behavioural, and social outcomes. A 2024 umbrella review of the impacts of ADHD summarised consistent associations with addiction, mental and physical illness, lower educational attainment, and social difficulties. Earlier reviews of Mendelian randomization studies of ADHD reached similar conclusions, reporting apparent causal effects on smoking, depression, body-mass index, and educational attainment. A broad two-sample Mendelian randomization analysis of ADHD across more than 100 traits corroborated these findings. Almost all of this genetic evidence, however, comes from samples of unrelated individuals, in which estimates can be confounded by population stratification, assortative mating, and dynastic effects. We searched PubMed and Google Scholar from database inception to 20/07/26 using terms related to ADHD, Mendelian randomization, and within-family designs (Supplementary note), without language restrictions. We identified eight relevant studies, however only three used a within-family or trio Mendelian randomization design. None used a large within-family Mendelian randomization design to investigate the effects of genetic liability to ADHD on health or behavioural outcomes while separating individuals liability from familial influences. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the largest within-family Mendelian randomization study of genetic liability to ADHD, comparing conventional population-based estimates with family-based estimates across 16 outcomes in up to 164,220 siblings. Population-based estimates reproduced previously reported associations, but most attenuated in family-based analyses. For depressive symptoms and age at first child, the two designs significantly differed, indicating that the population-based estimates were inflated by familial factors. Implications of all the available evidenceMuch of the excess health, behavioural, and social burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD arises, rather than an individuals own liability. If so, interventions directed solely at the individual may not reduce these outcomes as much as observational and population-based estimates imply. These findings should be interpreted alongside the broader evidence rather than as a basis for immediate changes in practice, and they underscore the need for larger family-based genetic studies.

papers.title: Interoceptive mechanisms of body image disturbance in anorexia nervosa: Study protocol of a randomized parallel-group trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundCurrent treatments for anorexia nervosa (AN), a dangerous psychiatric disorder, show only moderate efficacy. Interoceptive processing dysfunctions (i.e., how the brain receives and processes body afferents), and body image disturbance (BID) are clinical features of AN. Floatation-REST (Reduced Environmental Stimulation Therapy) has been reported to enhance both subjective interoceptive experiences and BID. The proposed project works to establish (1) how interoceptive processing dysfunctions may contribute to BID and (2) how the combination of Floatation-REST with psychotherapeutic principles may enhance interoceptive processing and BID in AN. MethodsIn this randomized parallel-group (NCT06332963), single-site trial, 102 women and girls with AN will be recruited from an inpatient program. After completing baseline measurements, participants are randomized on a 1:1 ratio to receive either the interoceptively focused treatment (IFT) or exteroceptively focused treatment (EFT) condition. Both conditions utilize acceptance- and mindfulness-based principles, however incorporate skills that focus on interoception or exteroception, respectively. Participants complete acute measures following each experimental therapeutic session, as well as post intervention, six-week and six-month follow-up. The primary outcome of the current study is acute changes in BID assessed by the Photographic Figure Rating Scale. Additional outcomes include acute changes in interoception, and longitudinal intervention effects on self-reported, behavioral, and neuroimaging measures of AN symptoms, BID, and interoception. DiscussionIf interventions demonstrate reductions in BID, mechanisms of BID will be further understood, informing the development of future therapies for BID in AN.

papers.title: Structural brain network organization and aggressive behavior in schizophrenia: a mega-analysis of 2260 patients and 3058 healthy controls from the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough most individuals with schizophrenia do not show aggressive behavior, rates are higher than in the general population. Identifying the neurobiological correlates of aggression may inform prevention. MethodsWe included 2260 individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 3058 healthy controls (HC) from 26 sites in the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group. The former were classified as showing at least moderate aggression (SZ+A; N = 231) or not (SZ-A; N = 2029) based on symptom rating scales. Structural covariance networks were constructed from cortical and subcortical volumes. We examined global and nodal network topology, as well as density within six large-scale brain networks and between each network and the rest of the brain. Metrics were summarized as the area under the curve (AUC) across a prespecified range of densities (K = 0.10-0.25, {Delta}K = 0.01). Group differences were assessed using pairwise permutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. ResultsGlobal and nodal network topology did not differ significantly between SZ+A and HC. Network-rest density of the salience network (SN) was higher in SZ+A than in HC, although this difference did not survive multiple-comparison correction ({Delta}AUC = 0.018, pBH = .083). In exploratory subgroup analyses, higher SN network-rest density was observed only in SZ+A with high delusion severity ({Delta}AUC = 0.021, p = .007). By contrast, SZ-A demonstrated extensive alterations in global network topology compared with SZ+A and HC, alongside selective alterations in nodal topology and large-scale network density compared with HC. Results were broadly consistent across sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions of aggression and adjusting for current antipsychotic dose. ConclusionsSZ+A was characterized by fewer--not more--abnormalities in structural covariance network organization than SZ-A, which may reflect etiological heterogeneity. In SZ+A with high delusion severity, higher network-rest density of the SN may point to aberrant salience processing in aggressive behavior.
